sections.h2: Tax offices at 223 North Spalding Avenue
sections.html:
Lebanon's county government offices for taxes sit under one address, 223 North Spalding Avenue, so a Marion County owner can finish most paperwork in a single trip. Suite numbers tell you where to go.

  • Sheriff's Office, Suite 101 (270-692-3051): bills and payments, open Monday to Friday between 8:30 and 4:30.
  • Property Valuation Administrator, Suite 202 (270-692-3401): value, name and address changes, and exemption applications, with the same Monday to Friday hours.
  • County Clerk, Suite 102 (270-692-2651): deed recording and delinquent bills. The clerk's own site lists 8:20 to 4:20 on weekdays and a Saturday morning session.

The sheriff passes valuation and bill-calculation questions to the PVA and sends anyone asking about delinquent bills, or about buying a lien, to the clerk.

Marion County is thinly settled: about 57 residents per square mile across 343 square miles of land. Lebanon, the seat, is the largest of three cities, followed by Loretto and Bradfordsville. One school district, Marion County Schools, serves every address.

Growth has been slow for a century. The population was 19,820 in 2010 and 19,581 in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate stands at 20,115, a 2.8 percent rise over the 2020 base. The county has 8,652 housing units and 7,724 households. Owners occupy 77.7 percent of homes, and more than nine in ten residents were at the same address a year earlier. The median home value is $168,100, median gross rent is $726, and owners with a mortgage pay a median of $1,243 a month. Building permits numbered 56 in 2025, so new construction adds little competition for a resale.

Selling a farm adds a twist. Under Section 172A of the state constitution, crop and pasture ground is valued by what it produces, while outbuildings and fencing are priced at what they would cost to replace, less wear. Ask the PVA how each of your acres is classed before you name a price.

Bills are mailed before October 1. Anyone still empty-handed on October 10 should phone the sheriff for a copy.

Marion County sheriff collection calendar
Payment windowWhat you pay
Oct. 1 to Nov. 1Printed amount minus two percent
Nov. 2 to Dec. 31Printed amount
All of JanuaryFive percent added
Feb. 1 to Apr. 15Twenty-one percent added
After Apr. 15Bill moves to the County Clerk

On April 16 whatever remains unpaid shifts to the County Clerk. The twenty-one percent adds the ten percent penalty of KRS 134.015 to the sheriff's collection add-on.

A mailed check should carry the bill number, and a stamped return envelope gets you a receipt. Cards work only at the counter, and the card company's charge falls on the cardholder. The system will not track a partial payment, so send the whole amount at once.

sections.h2: Who pays when the house sells
sections.html:
The person who owned the property on January 1 gets named on that year's bill. After a sale, the sheriff expects the seller to send the bill on to the buyer, and a buyer left without one can ask the office for a copy. The office carries no responsibility when a bill is missed during a closing.

Mortgage servicers are not sent a copy. The homeowner receives every bill and must hand it to the lender on time.

For earlier years, call the clerk at 270-692-2651. Overdue bills are transferred there, and the clerk's site advertises a free Online Deed Room. KRS 134.420 lets a tax lien stay on the land for eleven years, so a title company will insist that it be paid from the seller's proceeds.

Phone 270-692-3401 and request a sit-down. The meeting is the required first step of any appeal under state law, and KRS 133.120 then sends an unresolved case to the clerk as a written petition and on to a hearing. KRS 133.030 opens that hearing between 25 and 35 days after inspection wraps up.

State guidance has PVA staff inspect each Marion County parcel in person every four years or sooner, so find out when yours was visited. Appraisals and nearby sales carry weight. Payment stays due on the amount you claim.

Before the meeting, gather what a stranger would need to agree with you: photos of the house, an appraisal if you have one, repair estimates, and the prices of nearby homes that sold. Write down the value you think is fair and be ready to explain how you reached it. If the sit-down does not change the number, the petition to the clerk is your next step, and the clerk will tell you when the hearing is set.

The exemption removes $49,100 from the assessed value for 2025 and 2026. The PVA takes applications from owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled and who live in the house. About 19.5 percent of Marion County residents are 65 or older, so the exemption reaches a sizable share of owners. It stays with the owner, so a buyer applies separately. Bring proof of age or a disability classification when you file, and ask the PVA what else it wants to see so you only make one trip. If you sell mid-year, tell the PVA so the exemption does not linger on a house you no longer own.

sections.h2: Recording a deed at the clerk's counter
sections.html: The clerk first collects the grantor's transfer tax, which KRS 142.050 sets at fifty cents for every $500 of value or part of $500. Taxes paid at the clerk's counter can use cash, check, debit or credit card, and the clerk's site warns that cards carry extra fees. No tax is due on foreclosure sales, on transfers between spouses in a divorce, or on a parent's deed to a child for token payment.

sections.h2: Steps for a seller with a tax question
sections.html:
Start at the sheriff's counter in Suite 101 and ask whether the current year is paid. Then walk down the hall to the clerk in Suite 102 and ask whether any earlier year was transferred there. Last, stop at the PVA in Suite 202 to confirm the name and mailing address on the roll and whether a homestead exemption is on file.

Ask each office for the balance in writing and for the date through which the figure holds, since interest and penalties change the number as the calendar moves. Hand those letters to the title agent so each amount is paid out of your proceeds at closing. A cash sale can close quickly, so it helps to have the payoff papers in hand before you accept an offer.

If you inherited the property, check whose name the roll shows, and bring proof of your authority to act for the estate. The office will not guess who should receive a bill, so a name change on the roll keeps statements from going astray before the sale.

faqs.q: Where is the Marion County Sheriff's tax office?
faqs.a: It is at 223 North Spalding Avenue, Suite 101, in Lebanon, phone 270-692-3051. Mailed payments should show the bill number.

faqs.q: How much extra does a Marion County bill cost in February?
faqs.a: The sheriff adds 21 percent from February 1 to April 15, after 5 percent in January. Bills still open on April 16 go to the clerk.

faqs.q: Does the Marion County sheriff accept partial tax payments?
faqs.a: No. The sheriff's system does not track partial payments, so send the full bill in one payment.

faqs.q: Which office handles Marion County exemptions?
faqs.a: The PVA, at 270-692-3401. The sheriff refers homestead and disability questions there.

faqs.q: Where do I look up a Marion County delinquent bill?
faqs.a: Call the County Clerk at 270-692-2651. Delinquent bills are transferred to that office, and the clerk's site runs a free Online Deed Room.
